The rapid commoditization of frontier large language models (LLMs) has catalyzed the emergence of an alternative, cross-border secondary market for computational inference1. Operating as the computational counterpart to physical commodity bazaars such as 1688 and Taobao, this ecosystem arbitrates, aggregates, and redistributes raw token volume generated by premier artificial intelligence laboratories, including Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Alibaba Cloud1. Distributed across semi-private administrative panels, alternative developer forums, and decentralized communication channels, these token brokers consistently undercut Western retail application programming interface (API) list prices by 70% to 95%1.  
This secondary compute layer functions at the confluence of international regulatory friction, cross-border payment constraints, regional access controls, hyperscaler credit allocations, and programmatic reverse engineering2. For independent software engineers and gateway builders seeking cost-effective upstream endpoints, this ecosystem provides compute at scale2. However, these radical price reductions involve substantial trade-offs: extreme infrastructural instability, critical data confidentiality exposures, and active manipulation vectors, including token inflation ("token watering") and automated model substitution ("bait-and-switch" routing)2.

## **Structural Topology and Sourcing Mechanics of the Secondary Token Market**

The supply chain of the alternative token marketplace mirrors the tiered distribution models historically developed within decentralized proxy networks2. At the base of this structure are primary resource holders, colloquially designated as first-level account operators (*源头号商*)2. These entities specialize in the bulk acquisition, generation, and operational maintenance of raw compute credentials2. Upstream operators interface directly with cloud platforms, promotional grant pipelines, and subscription interfaces, absorbing the overhead of identity masking, account rotation, and anti-fraud evasion2.  
Directly downstream from primary resource holders sit the wholesale aggregators and intermediate resellers (*中转商 / 经销商*)2. These commercial entities operate multi-tenant routing panels that pool diverse upstream credentials, normalize varying response schemas into standard formats, manage customer billing, and resell throughput2. The final tier consists of downstream consumers (*耗商*), encompassing autonomous coding agents, independent software vendors, and developers who consume large volumes of tokens while seeking to bypass regional restrictions or retail pricing2.

| Upstream Sourcing Tier | Primary Technical Mechanism | Wholesale Discount vs. Retail | Structural Longevity | Upstream Fraud & Verification Risk |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Hyperscaler Credit Arbitrage** | Programmatic exploitation of AWS Activate, Azure Founders Hub, and Google Cloud startup allocations bound to Bedrock and Vertex AI2 | 50% to 80% discount2 | Weeks to months (terminates upon credit exhaustion or tenant audit)4 | High risk of sudden tenant termination; verifiable via cloud transport signatures4 |
| **Reverse-Engineered Developer Tool Protocols** | Extraction of session tokens and protocol emulation from developer tools such as Amazon Q Developer, Kiro IDE, and GitHub Copilot2 | 90% to 98% discount4 | Days to weeks (vulnerable to client protocol updates and upstream authentication patches)4 | Extreme vulnerability to upstream invalidation; fails cryptographic thinking-signature checks9 |
| **Web Session & Subscription Pools (Sub2API)** | Automation of consumer subscriptions (ChatGPT Plus/Team/Pro, Claude Pro/Max) via headless browser automation and OAuth extraction2 | 85% to 95% discount1 | Highly volatile (subject to strict rolling window rate limits and automated fraud bans)4 | High risk of silent capability degradation; stripped metadata and context truncation4 |
| **Domestic Asian Cloud Subsidies** | Sourcing wholesale domestic compute allocations via Alibaba Cloud DashScope, SiliconFlow, and direct DeepSeek nodes1 | 10% to 40% discount below global retail equivalents1 | Indefinite and contract-backed2 | Low risk; unadulterated official domestic cloud transport2 |
| **Enterprise Account Pooling (Pure Official / *官转*)** | Pooling Tier-4/Tier-5 enterprise organization keys with committed-use discounts2 | 0.8x to 1.5x of retail (priced at or slightly above retail for proxy access)4 | High stability and multi-month persistence2 | Minimal; 100% full-featured pass-through matching official benchmarks4 |

### **Hyperscaler Credit Arbitrage**

A foundational pillar of the secondary token trade rests on the systematic monetization of cloud startup credits2. Hyperscalers routinely allocate non-dilutive promotional vouchers ranging from $25,000 to over $100,000 to early-stage enterprises through incubators, accelerators, and venture programs14. Broker syndicates establish programmatic assembly lines using corporate shells, disposable business domains, and synthetic identities to secure these promotional allocations at scale14.  
Once credited, these accounts are dedicated to deploying managed foundation models, notably Anthropic Claude instances hosted on AWS Bedrock or Google Cloud Vertex AI, and OpenAI models hosted on Azure OpenAI Service4. Because the capital expenditure required to secure a voucher is negligible relative to the face value of the credit pool, resellers liquidate the compute at deep discounts2. The structural fragility of this model is high: hyperscaler fraud-detection systems continuously audit tenant resource consumption2. When an account exhibits anomalous API consumption patterns—such as non-stop streaming requests originating from untrusted autonomous system numbers—the account is terminated, severing downstream connections without notice4.

### **Reverse-Engineered Developer Tool Protocols**

A second sourcing pathway involves reverse-engineering programmatic endpoints embedded within developer-centric commercial applications2. Modern artificial intelligence coding environments, including Amazon Q Developer, the AWS-backed Kiro IDE, and GitHub Copilot, require background access to foundation models to power code completions and agentic workflows4. These tools communicate with upstream model servers using internal, non-public protocols that bypass standard retail API meters7.  
Open-source reverse-engineering frameworks, such as kiro-gateway and kiro2api, capture, de-obfuscate, and emulate the authentication handshakes of these client environments7. By wrapping these simulated sessions in standard HTTP server software, brokers expose an interface that accepts standard OpenAI or Anthropic payload schemas, converts them into proprietary tool payloads, injects harvested session credentials, and unwraps the resulting generation stream7. Because the underlying developer tools often bundle model compute into fixed-fee subscriptions or free preview programs, the marginal cost to the broker is virtually nonexistent4. Consequently, resellers distribute these streams at price multipliers as low as 0.05x of official rates4. However, this vector remains susceptible to sudden protocol modifications, client version enforcement, and server-side authentication patches deployed by platform maintainers4.

### **Web Session Pooling and Subscription-to-API Gateways**

Known across developer forums as "Sub2API" or "2API," this sourcing vector converts fixed-fee consumer subscriptions into programmatic API endpoints2. Consumer subscription tiers, such as ChatGPT Plus, Team, or Pro, and Claude Pro or Max accounts, offer fixed monthly pricing for high-volume conversational access2. Using open-source utilities such as Chat2API, fuclaude, and clove, brokers automate the extraction of session cookies, session tokens, and OAuth credentials11.  
The clove framework emulates the exact OAuth authentication handshakes utilized by official command-line interfaces such as Claude Code, providing access to extended model capabilities while evading per-token billing11. Upstream brokers maintain account pools (*池子*) containing dozens or hundreds of synchronized consumer accounts2. Inbound API requests are load-balanced across this pool4. When an individual account exhausts its rolling usage limit, the gateway rotates to the next available session4. This channel provides substantial cost savings but introduces severe quality-of-service risks: upstream platforms frequently deploy invisible browser-fingerprinting algorithms that throttle suspicious sessions, introduce latency jitter, or silently downgrade responses to smaller parameter checkpoints4.

### **Domestic Asian Cloud Subsidies and Bulk Official Commitments**

For non-Western foundation models—such as the DeepSeek architecture and Alibaba's Qwen model family—brokers source inference directly from regional hyperscalers and domestic compute aggregators1. Platforms such as Alibaba Cloud DashScope, SiliconFlow (*硅基流动*), and DeepSeek's native infrastructure operate in an environment characterized by aggressive compute subsidization and domestic enterprise competition2. Resellers leverage localized payment mechanisms, domestic corporate entity discounts, and high-tier volume commitments to purchase token volume at wholesale rates, repackaging the capacity for cross-border export2.  
Conversely, the premium tier of the underground compute market avoids synthetic or reverse-engineered sources entirely, relying on official enterprise accounts (*官转*)4. Operators in this segment aggregate official corporate API keys from Tier-4 and Tier-5 developer accounts with committed-use contracts2. These services provide identical performance to direct lab access, with no model swapping, prompt injection, or token manipulation4. Their pricing structures remain close to official retail benchmarks, occasionally commanding a 10% to 20% premium over retail to compensate the operator for providing cross-border payment processing, unblocking regional IP restrictions, and maintaining consolidated high concurrency limits2.

### **Public-Facing Aggregators: Architectural Footprints of APInex and Apixo**

Publicly accessible aggregator portals, exemplified by APInex (apinex.bond) and Apixo (apixoai.online), function as entry points for international developers seeking heavily discounted frontier compute1. APInex markets a consolidated, single-endpoint interface providing programmatic access to models from major AI labs alongside automated web research tools, advertising price points roughly ten times cheaper than standard retail rates18. Technical profiling reveals that APInex operates behind protective reverse-proxy networks deployed on Cloudflare infrastructure, utilizing top-level domains registered through privacy-preserving registrars (e.g., NicNames, Inc.) to obscure server origins and mitigate abuse-driven domain takedowns15.  
Apixo (apixoai.online) positions its infrastructure to support high-throughput coding agent workflows1. The platform advertises discounts up to 95% across foundational model families, including Claude 3.7 Sonnet, OpenAI's o-series, and DeepSeek variants, with baseline token rates starting at $0.04 per million tokens1. Onboarding is designed to eliminate standard commercial compliance barriers: developers authenticate directly through Telegram bots, receive instant provisioning with promotional testing balances, and top up their wallets exclusively using digital assets1.  
Crucially, Apixo implements native dual-wire format compatibility: incoming client traffic can communicate via the standard OpenAI /v1/chat/completions standard or Anthropic's native /v1/messages specification1. This architectural flexibility allows developers to integrate discounted upstream compute into complex client tools—including Claude Code, Cursor, Cline, OpenCode, and Roo Code—by modifying only the base URL parameter and authentication header, without requiring middleware schema translation1.

### **Software Management Engines: The New-API Ecosystem**

The underlying technical infrastructure powering modern alternative token panels is built on open-source gateway software5. While early operations relied on the Go-based One-API reference project, the ecosystem has converged on **New-API** (maintained by Calcium-Ion and the QuantumNous organization) as the standard management engine5. New-API provides a complete operational framework designed to aggregate disparate compute channels and redistribute them to multi-tenant user bases5:

* It provides an administrative interface for managing downstream client accounts, generating virtual API keys, enforcing quotas, configuring user-specific rate limits, and monitoring per-user margin yields5.  
* It incorporates an upstream channel management system capable of load-balancing traffic across hundreds of heterogenous compute sources, including raw developer keys, Azure endpoints, AWS Bedrock ARN interfaces, and reverse-proxy bridges5.  
* It includes an internal model-redirection and channel-weighting engine, allowing operators to map public-facing model aliases to arbitrary backend endpoints, implement weighted round-robin distribution, and establish automatic failover hierarchies when upstream nodes degrade5.  
* It handles on-the-fly protocol normalization, converting client-submitted JSON schemas into the syntax demanded by specific upstream providers while standardizing disparate Server-Sent Event (SSE) streams into standard formats6.

At the individual developer tier, desktop orchestration frameworks such as **CC Switch** have gained adoption2. Constructed using a Rust and Tauri architecture with local SQLite persistence, CC Switch operates as a local management node2. It allows developers to store credentials for dozens of competing reseller panels, monitor real-time latency across proxy nodes, configure client-side automatic failovers, and inject pre-configured environment parameters into terminal tools such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Gemini CLI2.

### **Underground Developer Clearinghouses**

The distribution, credential trading, and real-time operational monitoring of the reseller market occur within specialized online communities2. The primary forum for the Chinese-speaking token trade is **linux.do**, a technical community where upstream credential suppliers, middle-tier panel operators, and end developers interact2. On linux.do, suppliers negotiate bulk transactions of AWS credit accounts, trade session-generation scripts for developer IDEs, and review the uptime and packet fidelity of emerging proxy domains2.  
Outside structured developer forums, transactional volume flows through secondary e-commerce channels on Taobao and Xianyu (*闲鱼*)14. On these marketplaces, sellers package access to foundation models as pre-paid balance redemption codes, software development gift cards, or shared subscription seats14. This allows consumers to purchase computing power through domestic escrow rails without creating direct payment linkages to illicit proxy panels14.

## **Commercial Models, Multiplier Economics, and Financial Settlement Rails**

The commercial viability of secondary token platforms depends on a distinct pricing and billing architecture, supported by non-traditional financial settlement mechanisms1.

| Payment Settlement Rail | Counterparty Anonymity Level | Transaction Settlement Speed | Processing Surcharges | Regulatory & Chargeback Risk Profile |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Cryptocurrency & Stablecoins** (USDT on TRON, USDC on Arbitrum / Polygon)1 | High (completely unlinked from legal identity; no KYC required)1 | Automated execution upon 1 blockchain confirmation (~30–90s)1 | 0% to 1% network transfer fees1 | Immune to payment processor chargebacks, AML freezes, and card merchant bans1 |
| **Aggregated Fiat Micro-Merchant Gateways** (YiPay / *易支付*, Alipay / WeChat QR)2 | Low to Moderate (linked to domestic banking and corporate registries)2 | Instantaneous database crediting upon scan execution | 3% to 8% platform routing commission | Vulnerable to domestic payment gateway account suspension and business audit freezes2 |
| **E-Commerce Escrow Redemption Vouchers** (Taobao, Xianyu)14 | Moderate (shielded through marketplace consumer accounts)14 | Asynchronous (buyer inputs 32-character key into New-API panel)14 | Variable (marketplace merchant take-rates built into face value)14 | High platform-level moderation risk; listings frequently scrubbed by anti-abuse bots14 |

### **The Multiplier (*倍率*) Pricing Framework**

Unlike Western foundation model providers that bill using fixed dollar denominations per million tokens, the alternative reseller ecosystem calculates pricing through a mathematical abstraction inherited from the One-API codebase: the **Base Rate** combined with the **Model Multiplier** (*倍率*)5.  
The economic baseline for the entire ecosystem standardizes on a constant where one nominal platform dollar buys 500,000 standard computational tokens27. In the One-API convention that is stated as:

```text
base rate: 1 platform dollar = 500,000 base tokens
```

When an operator integrates an upstream compute channel into a New-API deployment, the billed amount for one request is:

```text
cost_usd = (prompt_tokens + completion_tokens * R) * M / 500000
```

where `M` is the specific **Model Multiplier** configured for that channel and `R` denotes the **Completion Ratio** (the price ratio of generation tokens relative to prompt tokens)27. The original draft carried these expressions only as inline images; they are restated here in text from the documented One-API convention, and the exact form of the original images could not be recovered. Treat the formula as a description of a convention, not as a verified vendor rate card.  
The Model Multiplier serves as the operator's primary pricing lever, calibrated to the acquisition cost of the underlying compute channel4. Pure official pass-through channels (*官转*) operate with multipliers set between 0.8x and 1.5x of official rates, delivering high fidelity at stable margins4. In contrast, channels backed by hyperscaler credit arbitrage operate at multipliers between 0.3x and 0.6x2.  
The lowest pricing tier—comprising reverse-engineered developer IDE endpoints and hijacked web sessions—is deployed with multipliers ranging from 0.01x to 0.2x4. In this bottom tier, operators leverage asymmetric completion ratios to mask costs27. By advertising low multipliers on input tokens while setting output multipliers to 3x or 4x, brokers present low entry costs while recovering margins during extended reasoning or code-generation workflows27.

### **Prompt Caching Arbitrage**

Advanced aggregators, such as Apixo, incorporate "cache-aware billing" into their commercial offerings1. Upstream foundation model providers discount prompt tokens by up to 90% when an identical context prefix is repeatedly submitted within a defined time window1.  
Secondary brokers exploit this mechanism across multi-turn agent workflows1. By maintaining persistent HTTP keep-alive connections and routing consecutive requests from a single client session to the exact same upstream physical tenant, the broker ensures that context caching triggers consistently on the upstream provider1. The aggregator bills the downstream user at an advertised discounted rate for cached prompts while capturing the full margin delta offered by the upstream lab, turning architectural state-preservation into direct operational profit1.

### **Financial Settlement Infrastructure**

To maintain operational continuity across jurisdictional borders, avoid capital controls, and circumvent financial fraud-detection systems, the reseller market relies on distinct payment rails1:

* **Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins:** International platforms prioritize digital asset transfers, accepting a spectrum of cryptocurrencies with a heavy concentration in stablecoins: USDT over the TRON (TRC-20) network and USDC across low-latency Ethereum Layer-2 networks, such as Arbitrum and Polygon1. Cryptographic settlement eliminates payment processing chargebacks, requires no Know-Your-Customer (KYC) documentation, and ensures real-time wallet crediting upon a single on-chain confirmation1. This allows platforms to pool cross-border revenue without exposure to banking freezes1.  
* **Aggregated Micro-Merchant Payment Gateways:** For developers inside regions subject to capital controls who lack cryptocurrency access, panels integrate domestic aggregator gateways (commonly known as YiPay / *易支付* frameworks)2. These systems route transactions through personal or shell-company QR codes on Alipay and WeChat Pay2. The transactions are labeled as generic software subscriptions, digital media downloads, or technical support vouchers, shielding the underlying compute transaction from payment processor scrutiny2.  
* **Platform-Escrowed Redemption Vouchers:** On consumer e-commerce platforms such as Taobao and Xianyu, brokers sell 32-character digital activation keys14. The customer purchases a listing for "Cloud Software Optimization Services," the vendor delivers the string via automated messaging, and the user enters the code into the New-API panel's redemption tab to instantly credit their account balance14. This mechanism uses consumer escrow protections while separating the payment rail entirely from the proxy server's domain infrastructure14.

## **Technical Architecture, Schema Transformation, and Model Integrity**

Operating an intermediary inference gateway requires active packet parsing, real-time schema translation, and stream reconstruction2. These technical interventions also introduce vectors for manipulation, prompting developer communities to build independent verification frameworks2.

| Manipulation Vector | Technical Implementation Mechanism | Observable Impact on Client Application | Primary Detection Benchmark |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Token Watering (*Token 注水*)** | Programmatic inflation of usage integers in the final JSON response or SSE metadata block2 | Wallet balance depletes 20% to 50% faster than calculated token usage2 | Local validation using offline tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken, Hugging Face Tokenizers)2 |
| **Model Substitution (*偷梁换柱*)** | Dynamic path rewriting in New-API; routing premium requests to cheaper open-weight or small models2 | Logic degradation, syntactic errors in code, loss of nuanced reasoning2 | Behavioral fingerprinting; cryptographic verification of thinking signatures6 |
| **Prompt Injection & Capability Nerfing (*降智 / 加料*)** | Automated injection of hidden system directives commanding the model to truncate responses2 | Unusually terse responses; refusal to generate comprehensive code blocks2 | System-prompt reflection probes; Canary injection audits2 |
| **Context Window Truncation** | Silent stripping of early message history blocks when conversation payloads exceed preset limits2 | Loss of long-range conversational memory; agent loops during multi-turn debugging4 | Needle-in-a-Haystack synthetic retrieval probes6 |

### **Protocol Translation Mechanics**

Because developer tooling is largely divided between OpenAI's REST conventions and Anthropic's Messages protocol, intermediate brokers implement comprehensive translation engines1. When a request targeting Anthropic's Claude 3.7 Sonnet is submitted using the OpenAI /v1/chat/completions schema, the gateway intercepts the JSON payload and restructures it prior to upstream transmission11:

* Top-level system messages contained within the messages array are parsed and extracted, converting them into the singular top-level system string required by Anthropic's API11.  
* Client tool definitions formatted under the OpenAI tools specification—including function schemas and parameters—are mapped into Anthropic's input_schema JSON definitions28.  
* For streaming interactions, the gateway parses upstream Server-Sent Event (SSE) frames4. It intercepts Anthropic events (e.g., content_block_start, content_block_delta, message_delta), strips provider-specific headers, and wraps the content fragments into OpenAI-compliant chat.completion.chunk structures9.  
* For reasoning-centric models, the gateway reconciles divergent paradigms9. It unwraps thinking content from DeepSeek-R1's <think> tags or Anthropic's structured thinking content blocks, mapping the traces to client-specified fields (such as reasoning_content) or prepending them directly into the standard response text9.

### **Adversarial Reseller Manipulation Vectors**

To preserve profit margins while selling tokens at steep discounts, disreputable operators deploy various manipulation strategies1:

* **Token Watering (*Token 注水*):** The proxy server intercepts the final JSON object emitted by the upstream provider and modifies the usage object2. By inflating prompt_tokens and completion_tokens values by 20% to 50% above actual counts, the platform debits the user's prepaid wallet at an accelerated rate, artificially lowering the nominal price per token while maintaining high realized margins2.  
* **Model Substitution (*偷梁换柱*):** The gateway's routing matrix inspects inbound requests targeting premium frontier models, such as Claude 3.7 Sonnet or OpenAI o32. If the prompt complexity appears low, the router silently redirects the request to a cheaper alternative—such as Claude Haiku, a domestic open-weight checkpoint (e.g., Qwen 2.5), or an aggressively quantized DeepSeek model2. The gateway then overrides the returning metadata, rewriting the response.model string to match the requested premium model2.  
* **Prompt Injection and Capability Nerfing (*降智 / 加料*):** To minimize computational overhead and limit completion token generation, brokers prepend hidden directives to the client's system prompt2. These instructions (e.g., *"Provide brief responses," "Avoid detailed explanations,"* or *"Limit output code to minimum essentials"*) restrict generation depth, degrading the model's analytical and reasoning capabilities2. Furthermore, to reduce memory overhead, platforms silently truncate conversation histories beyond arbitrary token limits, causing complex coding agents to lose context during multi-step tasks2.

### **Cryptographic and Behavioral Verification Frameworks**

To counter these manipulation vectors, independent developer communities have created verification tools, led by open-source projects such as **Veridrop** (canarybyte/veridrop), **CCTest** (cctest.ai), and the **BazaarLink Probe**2.  
The primary mechanism for verifying model authenticity is the validation of **Cryptographic Thinking Signatures**9. When extended thinking is invoked on authentic Anthropic Claude models, the response includes structured thinking blocks accompanied by an opaque signature field, typically spanning 500 to 2,000 characters9. This signature is generated using Anthropic's private cryptographic keys, securely binding the generated reasoning trace to the model9.  
When subsequent conversational turns are submitted that preserve prior thinking blocks, Anthropic's official API validates this signature9. If an intermediate reseller has substituted an inferior model, routed the request through an AWS Bedrock implementation that strips signatures, or used a reverse-engineered developer IDE endpoint (such as Kiro), the signature will be missing or invalid9. Replaying an invalid signature back to the official Anthropic API triggers an HTTP 400 Bad Request error9. Because resellers do not possess Anthropic's private signing keys, this cryptographic check cannot be forged9.  
Complementary verification techniques analyze protocol formatting and behavioral patterns:

* **Message ID Integrity:** Official Anthropic infrastructure enforces prefix conventions, including msg_ for standard conversational turns, toolu_ for client-side tool usages, and srvtoolu_ for server-executed operations10. Resellers running custom translation software or emulating endpoints frequently return generic UUIDs, exposing the presence of an unauthorized intermediary proxy10.  
* **Protobuf Transport Inspection:** Specialized diagnostic tools, such as CCTest, analyze raw streaming frames, decoding Protobuf signatures to determine whether compute originates from direct foundation model servers, enterprise cloud clusters (Bedrock or Vertex), or reverse-engineered developer IDE channels6.  
* **Residual Metadata Leaks:** In poorly constructed multi-model translation layers, gateways translating OpenAI requests to Claude backends inadvertently leak provider-specific fields (e.g., usage_source: anthropic returning inside an OpenAI response envelope), revealing proxy tampering10.

## **Operational Vulnerabilities and Risk Vectors**

Integrating secondary token brokers into production environments exposes applications to operational vulnerabilities spanning infrastructure stability, regulatory compliance, and data security2.

| Operational Risk Vector | Underlying Root Cause Mechanism | Severity Classification | Impact on Production Deployments |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Ephemeral Domain Churn** ("Month-Discard" Stations / *月抛站*)4 | Cloudflare suspensions, registry-level domain cancellations, and intentional operator exit-scams4 | **Critical** | Sudden endpoint non-resolution (DNS NXDOMAIN); complete loss of prepaid token balances4 |
| **Upstream Enforcement Waves** (*翻车* / Account Sweeps)2 | Automated fraud detection and risk controls deployed by foundation model providers2 | **High** | Cascades of HTTP 429 and 500 errors; overnight price increases of 200% to 400%2 |
| **Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Data Snooping**2 | Plain-text payload interception and database logging on untrusted intermediate servers2 | **Catastrophic** (Confidentiality) | Exfiltration of proprietary source code, internal system prompts, database credentials, and user data2 |
| **Packet Degradation & Streaming Stutter**4 | Multiplexing thousands of concurrent client connections over low-cost virtual private servers4 | **Moderate to High** | Dropped SSE completion events; client-side connection timeouts; corrupted JSON tool-call outputs4 |

### **The "Month-Discard" Operating Pattern and Exit Scams**

A significant segment of the lower-tier reseller market operates via disposable storefronts, termed "month-discard stations" (*月抛站*)4. These platforms operate on short lifecycles: they acquire disposable cloud credits or reverse-engineered accounts, collect prepaid customer balances via non-refundable crypto rails, run until upstream accounts are banned, and then abandon the domain4. Developers who maintain large prepaid balances on these services have no legal standing, lack enforceable Service Level Agreements (SLAs), and face sudden outages when the host domain goes offline2.

### **Upstream Compliance Crackdowns and Market Shocks**

Foundation model developers actively deploy automated systems to identify and terminate unauthorized traffic pooling2. When an AI lab updates its fraud-detection mechanisms—such as deploying behavioral analysis on Claude Code CLI sessions, fingerprinting proxy network autonomous systems, or tightening enterprise verification standards—the reseller supply chain experiences sudden supply contractions2.  
These enforcement sweeps trigger widespread account terminations across primary account farms (*翻车*)2. During an enforcement wave, secondary market pricing can surge significantly within hours, while requests fail with cascading HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) and HTTP 500 (Internal Server Error) status codes as proxy servers struggle to route traffic to exhausted key pools2.

### **Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) Data Confidentiality Risks**

The most severe threat to enterprise applications is the total compromise of data privacy2. To execute protocol conversions, calculate token usage, manage context caching, or apply prompt modifications, the intermediate gateway must terminate Transport Layer Security (TLS) and parse user prompts in plain text2.  
Because these entities operate outside recognized legal and regulatory frameworks (such as GDPR, SOC 2, or HIPAA), rogue proxy operators can log, analyze, or monetize user interactions2. Organizations routing developer or enterprise traffic through these relays risk exposing proprietary software repositories, internal database schemas, enterprise system prompts, and end-user personal data to untrusted third parties2.

## **Defensive Gateway Architecture for Independent Builders**

To leverage wholesale token pricing while insulating applications from upstream failures, developers must implement defensive routing architectures2. Production systems must treat alternative resellers as unverified, ephemeral compute backends, mitigating risk through redundant multi-provider failover, real-time circuit breaking, and out-of-band cryptographic verification2.

```yaml
# Illustrative LiteLLM router configuration. Example only: it has not been
# validated against a running deployment, and the relay endpoints below are
# placeholders. Substitute an endpoint you have vetted yourself.
# Model ids are examples; the authoritative catalog is provider sync output.
# Pattern: discounted relay tiers plus a contractual official fallback.

model_list:  
  # Primary Routing Tier: High-discount alternative compute broker  
  - model_name: claude-3-7-sonnet  
    litellm_params:  
      model: openai/claude-3-7-sonnet  
      api_base: https://<primary-relay-base>/v1  
      api_key: os.environ/PRIMARY_RELAY_API_KEY  
      rpm: 120  
      tpm: 400000  
      max_retries: 1  
      timeout: 12

  # Secondary Routing Tier: Alternative backup reseller channel  
  - model_name: claude-3-7-sonnet-backup  
    litellm_params:  
      model: openai/claude-3-7-sonnet  
      api_base: https://<secondary-relay-base>/v1  
      api_key: os.environ/SECONDARY_RELAY_API_KEY  
      rpm: 60  
      tpm: 200000  
      max_retries: 1  
      timeout: 12

  # Fallback Safety Net: Official enterprise API (committed-use, unadulterated)  
  - model_name: claude-3-7-sonnet-official  
    litellm_params:  
      model: anthropic/claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219  
      api_key: os.environ/ANTHROPIC_OFFICIAL_API_KEY  
      rpm: 2000  
      tpm: 1600000  
      timeout: 30

router_settings:  
  # Route traffic based on observed real-time response latency  
  routing_strategy: latency-based-routing  
  routing_strategy_args:  
    lowest_latency_buffer: 0.20  
    ttl: 120

  # Reliability, circuit breaking, and automated cooldown configuration  
  num_retries: 2  
  allowed_fails: 2               # Trip circuit breaker after 2 consecutive failures  
  cooldown_time: 30              # Quarantine an unstable endpoint for 30 seconds  
  enable_pre_call_checks: true   # Validate rate limits and context bounds pre-flight

  # Deterministic failover topology: Primary -> Secondary -> Official Direct  
  fallbacks:  
    - claude-3-7-sonnet:  
        - claude-3-7-sonnet-backup  
        - claude-3-7-sonnet-official

  # Handle context window overages gracefully across providers  
  context_window_fallbacks:  
    - claude-3-7-sonnet: ["claude-3-7-sonnet-official"]

general_settings:  
  master_key: os.environ/GATEWAY_ADMIN_KEY  
  database_url: os.environ/REDIS_ROUTER_STATE_URL
```

### **Automated Auditing and Synthetic Verification Daemons**

To defend production environments against silent model swapping, prompt injection, and token inflation, builders deploy background verification daemons that run continuously alongside user traffic2.

### **Integrity checks a buyer can run**

The earlier draft of this section carried a Python "canary daemon" that claimed to verify cryptographic thinking signatures out of band. It was removed rather than repaired: its verification function discarded the signature and returned a length check, so it reported success without verifying anything, and its own docstring called itself a simulation. A length check on an opaque token is not evidence of model identity.

What genuine verification would require, in order of strength:

1. **Signature replay.** When extended thinking is enabled, the vendor attaches a server-signed thinking block. Replaying a preserved block to a party that validates it, and observing acceptance versus `400`, tests whether the signature came from the vendor's key. This detects a relay that strips or forges the block. It does not detect a relay that forwards genuine signed content produced by a different model, so it is necessary but not sufficient.
2. **Identifier shape.** Official turns use `msg_`, tool calls `toolu_`, server-side tools `srvtoolu_`. Generic UUIDs indicate a translation layer, which is normal for a gateway and not by itself evidence of substitution.
3. **Tokenizer agreement.** Token counts recomputed locally with the vendor's tokenizer should match reported `usage` within the vendor's documented accounting rules. Divergence on a stable prompt is the observable signature of token inflation.
4. **Deterministic recall.** A fixed needle-retrieval prompt repeated across the advertised context window detects silent truncation.

No verification tool is implemented in this repository, and this document does not claim one is. These are recorded as the checks that would turn the claims above into measurements.

```text
signal                      what it can show              what it cannot show
signature replay            block stripped or forged      wrong model with genuine block
identifier shape            translation layer present     whether output is honest
tokenizer agreement         usage inflation                which model produced text
recall probe                context truncation             model identity
```

## **Strategic Conclusions and Architectural Directives**

The underground wholesale compute market presents an asymmetric trade-off for independent gateway builders1. It provides access to high-throughput frontier inference at 70% to 95% below retail pricing, creating compelling unit economics for compute-heavy applications1.  
However, because these discounts are enabled by cloud credit arbitrage, protocol reverse engineering, and subscription pooling, the operational foundation of this ecosystem remains inherently volatile2:

* **Strict Workload Segmentation:** Reseller endpoints must never be used to process proprietary source code, personally identifiable information, or regulated enterprise data2. Their utility is restricted to cost-sensitive, non-sensitive tasks: synthetic training data generation, large-scale web scraping extraction, and background evaluation pipelines.  
* **Defensive Gateway Topologies:** Production architectures must avoid single-provider dependencies. Resellers should be abstracted behind local management layers (e.g., LiteLLM) configured with short request timeouts, strict circuit-breaking policies, and automatic fallback pathways to official, contract-backed provider accounts33.  
* **Continuous Zero-Trust Verification:** Gateways must treat all upstream compute as unverified by default. Automated auditing pipelines should continuously track token inflation, validate message ID schemas, and verify cryptographic thinking signatures to ensure the delivery of genuine frontier model outputs2.

## **Evidence Status**

No claim in this document is a primary measurement. Each citation number resolves to one of three classes:

| Class | What it establishes | Examples here |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Vendor self-claim** | What a supplier advertises. Evidence of marketing, never of delivery. | Sources 1 and 18 (the two aggregator storefronts), 22 (New-API's own repository), 19 (a relay probe run by a third party on a vendor endpoint). |
| **Secondary report** | A third-party write-up, forum post, blog or video. Useful for vocabulary and reported practice. | Sources 2, 4, 5, 7, 14, 25, 32 and most of the remainder. |
| **Unmeasured** | Asserted with no usable source, or a number with no stated method. | The 0.05x–0.2x multiplier bands, the "20% to 50%" token-watering range, the months-to-weeks longevity estimates, and every percentage that appears without a sample or date. |

What follows from that table:

- The 70–95% discount band is a storefront's own advertised range, not an observed price distribution.
- The sourcing taxonomy is a **reported** taxonomy. This document did not acquire, test or verify any of the supply channels it describes, and it does not instruct the reader to do so.
- The integrity-check section describes methods that would produce evidence; none was executed to produce this document.
- Where this document and its companion strategy document both cite the same supplier pages, that is one source quoted twice, not corroboration.
